raw: {"slots": {"question": [{"claim": "The paper asks how online partisan polarization about COVID-19 measures varies across U.S. states and Canadian provinces, and how it relates to political leaning, conspiracy content, and vaccination rates.", "quotes": [{"text": "Specifically, we analyze millions of tweets to determine how polarization correlates with: (1) the ideological leanings of different regions; (2) exposure to conspiracy theory-related content; and (3) vaccination rates.", "page": 3}]}, {"claim": "The paper asks whether language dissimilarity between partisan groups on the same contentious topic reflects polarization, rather than just each group's own lexicon.", "quotes": [{"text": "language dissimilarity between different partisan groups more likely reflects alternative semantic understandings of that specific topic", "page": 4}]}, {"claim": "The paper asks whether polarization in online discourse changes over time and how quickly, finding that spikes tied to political events are short-lived.", "quotes": [{"text": "These polarization surges typically lasted only a few days, revealing the dynamic nature of online partisan discourse.", "page": 1}]}, {"claim": "The paper asks whether online discussions only reflect public opinion or may also help drive changes in it, and it suggests they potentially do both.", "quotes": [{"text": "Our findings suggest that online discussions both reflect and potentially drive rapid", "page": 1}]}], "central_claim": [{"claim": "Politically conservative regions show significantly higher partisan polarization in online COVID-19 discussion in both countries, more strongly in the U.S., and U.S. regional vaccination rates are strongly negatively correlated with polarization in vaccine discussions.", "quotes": [{"text": "Our analysis reveals that politically conservative regions exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization in both countries, with this effect particularly pronounced in the United States.", "page": 1}, {"text": "We demonstrate a strong negative correlation between regional vaccination rates and the degree of polarization in vaccine-related discussions in the U.S., suggesting tangible public health implications of online partisan division.", "page": 1}]}], "evidence": [{"claim": "The main corpus is COVID-19 political tweets from the U.S. and Canada, collected from a 1% Twitter API sample between October 9, 2020 and January 4, 2021.", "quotes": [{"text": "We collected a large-scale dataset of COVID-19 political discussions on Twitter (now X) occurring between October 9, 2020, to January 4, 2021, comprising approximately 12.5 million tweets linked to the United States and 46.6 million tweets linked to Canada.", "page": 4}]}, {"claim": "Vaccination outcomes come from official rates recorded about a year after the Twitter collection period, because vaccines were not available during it.", "quotes": [{"text": "We used officially reported vaccination rates from one year after our Twitter data collection period, as COVID-19 vaccines were only created and approved at the very end of our initial data collection.", "page": 5}]}, {"claim": "Party labels for U.S. users were checked against voter registration records from five states and DC.", "quotes": [{"text": "we matched Twitter users with primary voter registration records available for five states (Ohio, New York, Florida, Arkansas, North Carolina) and Washington DC.", "page": 8}]}, {"claim": "User locations were inferred from free-text profile location fields, using OpenStreetMap and ArcGIS coordinates, and the resulting regional counts correlate strongly with official census population data.", "quotes": [{"text": "We processed this free-form text field using Open Street Map and the ArcGIS API, which both return latitude and longitude coordinates when a location is found.", "page": 6}]}, {"claim": "COVID-19 epidemic data consist of officially reported new cases and deaths from the CDC for the U.S. and from the Canadian government for Canada.", "quotes": [{"text": "We used officially reported COVID-19 new cases and death data from each country.", "page": 5}]}, {"claim": "Topic relevance was defined partly through hashtags: about 18,000 U.S. and 3,600 Canadian hashtags were ranked by frequency, and two political scientists labelled 631 as relevant.", "quotes": [{"text": "Two political scientists manually annotated this list with topic and relevance labels, narrowing it to 631 relevant hashtags.", "page": 5}]}, {"claim": "Party affiliation was assigned with a two-step method: a RoBERTa-large classifier trained on profile text, whose labels then supervised an activity-based classifier that uses averaged tweet embeddings.", "quotes": [{"text": "Using an 80−20 train-test split, we then trained a RoBERTa-large model to determine user party affiliation based on profile text.", "page": 8}]}, {"claim": "Inferred party affiliation was externally checked against official election results, with the ratio of liberal to conservative labelled users per region correlating at 0.802 for the U.S. and 0.815 for Canada.", "quotes": [{"text": "For the U.S. and Canada, we calculated the correlation between the ratio of liberal to conservative-labeled users per region in our dataset compared to official election results, obtaining strong correlations of 0.802 for the United States and 0.815 for Canada", "page": 8}]}, {"claim": "The polarization measure is based on the distance between partisan users' language in a RoBERTa embedding space, scored with the C-index clustering measure.", "quotes": [{"text": "We then measure polarization by quantifying how far apart the language of left and right-leaning users is positioned in this embedding space, using the C-index [42], a robust clustering measure.", "page": 4}]}], "key_findings": [{"claim": "Conservative states and provinces show higher polarization than counterparts.", "page": 13}]}, {"claim": "In the U.S., vaccine polarization is strongly negatively correlated with actual vaccination rates across states.", "quotes": [{"text": "Importantly, we Canada, which the authors attribute to small sample size and vaccine mandates.", "quotes": [{"text": "We did not observe a similar pattern in Canada, due to small sample size and the implementation of vaccine mandates.", "page": 16}]}, {"claim": "Aggregate polarization rises and decays quickly around peaks, on a timescale of days.", "quotes": [{"text": "This aggregate analysis (Fig 14c) confirms a rapid, symmetric rise-and-decay profile around polarization peaks, occurring on timescales of days.", "page": 19}]}, {"claim": "In the U.S., daily polarization is weakly but significantly negatively authors state that their results are correlational and do not imply causation.", "quotes": [{"text": "Finally, while several of our analyses rely on correlations, these results do not imply causation.", "page": 25}]}, {"claim": "Because the sample is of politically engaged Twitter users, the findings describe a vocal subset of online discourse rather than the general public.", "quotes": discourse.", "page": 24}]}, {"claim": "The authors did not find the U.S. vaccine-polarization pattern in Canada, and they attribute this to small sample size and vaccine mandates, so the Canadian pattern is not established.", "quotes": [{"text": "We did not observe a similar pattern in Canada, due to small sample size and the implementation of vaccine mandates.", "page": 16}]}, {"claim": "Because the Twitter data were collected in late 2020 and vaccination rates come from 2021, the link between vaccine polarization and later uptake is only suggestive and reflects a possible predictive relationship, not a demonstrated one.", "quotes": [{"text": "As a result, correlations between polarization in vaccine-related discussions and later vaccination uptake should be understood as suggestive rather than causative.", "page": 25}]}, {"claim": "The Canadian analysis is limited to English-language tweets, so it mainly reflects anglophone or bilingual francophone views, which may bias results such as those for Quebec.", "quotes": [{"text": "we restricted our analysis to English-language tweets, which in Canada means we primarily captured perspectives of either anglophones or bilingual francophones", "page": 24}]}, {"claim": "The keyword strategies differed between the U.S. and Canadian datasets, so the cross-national comparison of polarization patterns should be interpreted with caution.", "quotes": [{"text": "This asymmetry may have contributed to cross-national differences in patterns of observed polarization, and this should be considered when interpreting the comparative results.", "page": 25}]}, {"claim": "The timing of the event-linked polarization peaks is not evidence of causal effects of those events; the peaks only coincide with contentious events.", "quotes": [{"text": "While direct causal evidence is not available, we find that many of the largest polarization peaks coincide with highly contentious events specific to each country’s context.", "page": 17}]}, {"claim": "The Canadian regional associations between polarization and conservative vote share were not statistically significant, which the authors partly attribute to having few regions.", "quotes": [{"text": "For Canada, these associations are not statistically significant, partly due to the smaller number of regions analyzed.", "page": 16}]}], "theoretical_positioning": [{"claim": "The authors position the work within text-embedding approaches to polarization and choose a strictly text-based method over network-based ones, which they say are becoming restricted.", "quotes": [{"text": "Consequently, our study adopts a strictly text-based method, which remains both accessible and scalable for analyzing large-scale digital discourse.", "page": 3}]}, {"claim": "The authors present embedding-based models as complementing lexicon-based strategies, which they build on in their method.", "quotes": [{"text": "Embedding-based models capture latent semantic distinctions between ideological groups, providing methodological advantages that complement traditional lexicon- or dictionary-based strategies.", "page": 3}]}, {"claim": "The authors present their work as extending earlier studies of regional partisan divides by adding geographic and temporal analysis tied to events.", "quotes": [{"text": "However, we extended beyond these studies to characterize the geographic heterogeneity and temporal evolution of polarization, connecting features in our polarization metric to real-world events.", "page": 22}]}, {"claim": "The authors treat language dissimilarity between partisan groups as insufficient evidence of polarization on its own, because each group has its own lexicon. They argue that dissimilarity on the same contentious topic is a better signal, which is why they condition on topic.", "quotes": [{"text": "Therefore, dissimilar language alone does not necessarily indicate polarized positions.", "page": 4}, {"text": "However, when examining discussions on the same contentious topic, language dissimilarity between different partisan groups more likely reflects alternative semantic understandings of that specific topic—a phenomenon we hypothesize correlates strongly with polarization.", "page": 4}]}, {"claim": "The authors accept semantic similarity as only a proxy for partisan polarization and acknowledge that this proxy may miss signals that embedding representations do not capture.", "quotes": [{"text": "First, we measured partisan polarization only through the proxy of semantic similarity, which may in certain cases obscure signals not captured by semantic embedding representations.", "page": 24}]}], "interlocutor_claim": [{"claim": "Owen et al. (ref. 94) reported reduced negative sentiment in Canadian vaccine-related tweets during 2020; the authors contrast their own finding that polarization was not negatively correlated with conspiracy tweet volume in Canada.", "quotes": [{"text": "This contrasts with [94], who found reduced negative sentiment in Canadian vaccine-related tweets between January and December 2020.", "page": 24}]}, {"claim": "Merkley et al. (ref. 103) describe a rare cross-partisan consensus among Canadians on emergency pandemic measures early on; the authors contrast this with social media, where that consensus was not mirrored and conspiracy theories circulated.", "quotes": [{"text": "Indeed, there was a rare “crosspartisan consensus” among Canadians regarding emergency measures in the early stages of the pandemic [103].", "page": 24}, {"text": "This consensus, however, was not mirrored on social media, where conspiracy theories widely circulated [24,95].", "page": 24}]}, {"claim": "Burns et al. (ref. 96) are cited for the finding that vaccine hesitancy in Canada was linked to political affiliation, with Conservative Party supporters more likely to refuse vaccination; the authors present this as a parallel to the U.S. pattern.", "quotes": [{"text": "Like in the U.S., vaccine hesitancy was linked to political affiliation in Canada, with Conservative Party supporters more likely to refuse vaccination [96].", "page": 24}]}, {"claim": "The introduction states that extensive prior research confirms U.S. Democratic supporters were more consistently likely than Republicans to follow social distancing guidelines, a finding the paper uses as background for its study of partisan divides.", "quotes": [{"text": "Extensive research now confirms that in the U.S., Democratic Party supporters were consistently more likely to adhere to social distancing guidelines [8–10]", "page": 2}]}, {"claim": "The authors say their main finding, that conservative states showed higher polarization in response to public health interventions, is consistent with earlier studies (refs. 10 and 62) that reported the same pattern relative to liberal states.", "quotes": [{"text": "This main finding is consistent with previous studies suggesting conservative states exhibited higher polarization (Fig 11) in response to public health interventions compared to liberal counterparts [10,62].", "page": 23}]}]}}
